github.title: kajisho5/ffmpeg-skill
github.abstract:
Give your coding agent a video editor. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client edits your footage with local FFmpeg, then checks its own output. No cloud · No API keys · Python standard library Website · Quick start · Demos · Tools · MCP · npm npx ffmpeg-skill caption.py --animate pop --karaoke fit.py --aspect 9:16 --fit crop silence.py --threshold -35 loudness.py -I -14 --tp -1 Left half is the input, right half is what the command produced. Every before/after demo, with the exact command under each one → — all of it built by python3 demos/build.py , so you can rebuild every frame of it yourself. The footage is synthetic (FFmpeg's own test sources) except in three demos, reframe_talk , filler_en and pauses_en , which use two AI-generated clips of people who do not exist ( demos/footage/ ). ffmpeg-skill is an Agent Skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and any agent that reads SKILL.md . It teaches the agent a fixed workflow (probe → edit losslessly where possible → check → verify) and ships 42 tools that do the actual work with ffmpeg / ffprobe : cut, join, silence removal, fit to duration and aspect, captions and karaoke, overlays and motion graphics, HDR → SDR and LUTs, audio clean-up and typed dynamics, sync with drift correction, multicam, loudness, delivery checks, whole-edit project rendering, batch folders. Every tool is also callable as an MCP tool ( tools/list advertises a core 12 by default to keep client context small, with FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1 listing all 42; every tool is reachable by name through tools/call either way), and the whole set is described by a machine-readable contract. If ffmpeg and python3 are on your PATH, it works: offline, on footage you would rather not upload. SPEC (Self-Producing Execution Contract): each tool's input_schema — the part of its
contract and MCP tool definition that has to track the CLI flag-for-flag — is never
hand-authored beside the code. It is derived, at run time, from the same argparse parser that
already defines the CLI, and CI fails the build if any of it drifts.
→ full explanation Standalone, and in an ecosystem Standalone , this is a local FFmpeg engine: probe → edit → verify, npx ffmpeg-skill and nothing else. No API key, no account, no other repo required. Everything above and below this section describes that standalone tool, and none of it changes if you never read the rest of this one. In kajisho5 's wider video-production ecosystem , this repo is the hands : it cuts, measures and exports files, and reports back in structured JSON. It does not decide what to cut, whether a deliverable is approvable, what makes a highlight interesting, or what a caption should say (the user's cue text is burned as written, never rewritten to fit) — those are a brain 's job, sitting in front of this engine, not inside it. You want to... Use Cut / join / measure / export a file right now this repo ( ffmpeg-skill ), standalone Decide cut points, approve a deliverable, plan a whole edit video-production-agent / AI-video-production-OS Build a typed editing graph across a workspace, without writing raw ffmpeg video-editing-skill / audio-production-skill Put Remotion motion graphics (animated captions, silence jump cuts, audio-peak motion) on a real recording remotion-ffmpeg-skill : its compositions take their length, fps, frame, silences, scene cuts, audio peaks and beats from this repo's probe.py , silence.py and scenes.py . It verifies its render with check.py and look.py , composites a graphics layer with overlay.py ( --place for its --sparse mode), and delivers through render.py --template Other repos in the ecosystem — media-analysis-skill , transcription-skill , subtitle-skill , thumbnail-skill , color-grading-skill , motion-graphics-skill , qc-skill — read this repo's contract --json , its tools' --json output and doctor , the same way any agent framework would; this repo does not call into any of them. The dependency runs one way. Contents Standalone, and in an ecosystem · Why · Quick start · How it works · Design principles · Tools · Audio · Built for agents · FAQ · FFmpeg compatibility · Tested on real footage · Install · Requirements · Development · Docs Why An agent that "knows FFmpeg" still guesses: it assumes a frame rate, picks a codec the container cannot hold, re-encodes a file that only needed a stream copy, and reports "done" without opening the result. This skill takes the guessing out: Real files first. Every job starts with probe.py ; the agent decides from the measured duration, fps, resolution, colour and audio layout, not from the file name. Structured tools, not shell strings. Each operation is a script with typed arguments. Nothing runs through a shell; no filter graph is accepted from the caller. A contract the agent can read. contract --json states, for every tool, what it takes, what it writes, which FFmpeg components it needs and how the result is verified. The MCP surface is derived from it. Verification after execution. The result is probed, checked against the destination's spec and, when the picture changed, looked at as a contact sheet. Local first. No cloud, no API keys, no Python dependencies. Optional local transcription is used when a speech engine (Parakeet or a whisper) is installed, never required — by caption.py --transcribe and, since 1.17, by silence.py --transcribe (with --filler , or since 3.6 with --sentence-min-silence / --sentence-margin-tail ); both take a transcript you already have instead, and both refuse with the install lines rather than guessing. Both take --engine and --model ; FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_ENGINE and FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_MODEL set this machine's defaults (e.g. large-v3-turbo where that whisper.cpp model is installed; without either, auto and base ). The engine runs on your machine and the audio is never uploaded; parakeet-mlx, faster-whisper and openai-whisper download their model weights the first time they run (parakeet-mlx's default from Hugging Face). Paper The design discipline behind this skill — per-operation verification for AI agents — is written up as a position paper. The paper scores ffmpeg-skill itself as only partially conformant with the discipline it defines. Kajiyama, S. (2026). What Is Verification-Driven Coding? — A Discipline for Not Trusting Generation. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23720216 Quick start # 0. FFmpeg itself, once (Ubuntu/Debian shown; macOS and Windows are in the Install table below) sudo apt install ffmpeg # 1. install the skill for Claude Code (Cursor: --cursor, Codex: --codex, all three: --all) npx ffmpeg-skill # 2. check the machine: ffmpeg, ffprobe and every FFmpeg component the tools need npx ffmpeg-skill doctor # 3. (for agent frameworks) read the machine-readable contract npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json | head -40 Captions from speech ( caption.py --transcribe ) need one local speech engine, installed separately. pip install faster-whisper is the simplest; the first run downloads its model, and the audio never leaves the machine. Without an engine, everything else works, doctor lists the engine as missing optional, and --transcribe refuses with the install line for each engine it supports. Already installed? re-run npx ffmpeg-skill to refresh ~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill . Copies are not updated automatically. doctor 's overall ok and a single tool's usable are different signals: ok is false when anything some tool requires is missing, so one missing filter (a plain Homebrew ffmpeg without subtitles , or a build without libvidstab) turns it false even though most tools still run. Check doctor --json 's tools field for the per-tool answer, not just ok . Then talk to your agent: "Take interview.mp4 , keep 0:45–3:10 and 5:00–6:30, and make it exactly 60 seconds for Reels." The agent runs probe.py , cut.py --segments 0:45-3:10,5:00-6:30 , fit.py --duration 60 --aspect 9:16 --fit crop , export.py --preset reels , check.py --platform reels and look.py , then reports "final.mp4: 59.

github.abstract:
The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents. Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines. Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português ① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output. Test runs, diffs, logs and builds are compressed before your agent reads them. 100+ commands, under 25 ms per command, no config, nothing changes in how you work. rtk gain shows what you saved. ② Go further with pipelines, as far as you take it. Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own.
The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its author's benchmark . Agents across the whole company? RTK Pro is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. Discover RTK Pro ↓ Install & forget macOS, and Linux with Homebrew brew install rtk Windows, with winget winget install rtk-ai.rtk Linux, macOS or WSL, with the install script curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh Then plug it into your agent rtk init -g # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent" Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs git status , RTK runs rtk git status and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this. Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: rtk gain must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found". Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: Installation guide · per-agent setup and --dry-run : Quick Start Measure it: rtk gain Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it. rtk gain # Summary stats rtk gain --graph # ASCII graph (last 30 days) rtk gain --history # Recent command history rtk gain --daily # Day-by-day breakdown rtk gain --all --format json # JSON export for dashboards rtk discover # Find missed savings opportunities rtk discover --all --since 7 # All projects, last 7 days rtk session # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions What the numbers mean. The compressor reduces the command output your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as bytes / 4 , so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate. After a week of data, rtk gain ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. pro_hint = false under [display] in config.toml turns it off. Full explanation: How RTK Savings Work · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: Token Savings Analytics Out of the box: the bash compressor The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship. Operation What the agent reads cargo test / npm test / pytest / go test Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count git status / git diff / git log Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit git add/commit/push A confirmation line instead of progress output ls / tree / grep / rg Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut ruff check / eslint / cargo clippy Grouped by rule and file docker ps / kubectl Essential fields only 100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: What RTK Optimizes Three promises Never blocks. If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged. Never worse. RTK never prints more than the command did. Nothing hidden. Output that is cut says where the full version is, and rtk bypass runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in rtk gain : rtk bypass git log --oneline -20 # full git log, no truncation rtk bypass npm install express # raw npm output The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as Read , Grep and Glob pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see Pipelines below). Does RTK break the prompt cache? No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. Details . Want to go further? Pipelines. Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out. What people turn on first Compress everything the agent reads , not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code). Hand big file reads to a cheaper model you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key). Clean the API traffic your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below). Make the agent write less : terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent). Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. rtk-ai.app/pipelines lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command: rtk pipeline add github:user/repo # check and install a shared pipeline A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: Agent Coverage shows what runs where. Start here: Pipelines · the built-ins, explained: Reference Pipelines · write and share your own: Writing a Pipeline , Pipeline Commands RTK Proxy (optional) The rtk-proxy daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's provider-API traffic : it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in rtk gain . rtk init -g offers to set it up; rtk claude starts it and launches Claude through it with no configuration at all. rtk claude # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it rtk llm-proxy status # is it up rtk gain # savings, command filtering and proxy side by side Separate binary, separate licence (BUSL-1.1), its own rtk-proxy-<target> archive: rtk never links it. Not the same thing as rtk bypass , which runs one local command unfiltered. Setup and subcommands: RTK Proxy · what it compresses: What the Proxy Compresses · settings and endpoints: Proxy Configuration Agents across the whole company? Know what they cost, what they touch, and who ran what. RTK runs on each developer's machine. RTK Pro connects them into one control layer for the whole company: Gateway. Every AI call goes through one place, whichever provider each team uses. Cost control. Spend by team, person and model. Waste found and removed. Budgets that warn, then stop. Shield. Secrets and personal data masked before any model sees them. Policies. Risky commands stopped before they run. Team catalog. Skills, MCP servers and pipelines, assigned per team and project. Audit log. Who did what, and whether it was allowed. Nothing changes for the developer. No secret value ever leaves the machine.

github.abstract:
Quickstart · Headroom for Teams · Install · Proof · Agents · Docs · Discord · llms.txt AI agents / LLMs: read /llms.txt here, or fetch the live index · full docs blob . Headroom ( headroom-ai on PyPI and npm) compresses everything your AI agent
reads — tool outputs, logs, RAG chunks, files, and conversation history — before
it reaches the LLM. Same answers, fewer input tokens. Measured: 21–57% fewer
input tokens on four agent scenarios, 90%+ on repeated JSON arrays and log
lines, little on prose ( Proof ). Compression
runs on your machine; no prompt or file content is sent anywhere to be compressed. Start here My app calls an LLM (Python, LangChain, LiteLLM, Agno, Strands): pip install headroom-ai from headroom import compress result = compress ( messages , model = "gpt-4o" ) # OpenAI or Anthropic message dicts client . chat . completions . create ( model = "gpt-4o" , messages = result . messages ) No API key, no model download, in-process. Set HEADROOM_OFFLINE=1 for a
zero-network run. Tool and assistant messages are compressed; user messages are
left alone unless you pass compress_user_messages=True . FastAPI example · API reference .
TypeScript apps: npm install headroom-ai plus the proxy
( pip install "headroom-ai[proxy]" , headroom proxy --port 8787 ); the npm SDK
sends messages to it. TypeScript quickstart I run coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode, Aider): uv tool install --python 3.13 " headroom-ai[all] " headroom wrap claude Zero code changes. Agent compatibility · Proxy 10,144 → 1,260 tokens. The same FATAL found. What it does Library — compress(messages) in Python or TypeScript, inline in any app. Proxy — headroom proxy --port 8787 , zero code changes, any language. Agent wrap — headroom wrap claude|codex|grok|copilot|cursor|aider|opencode|cline|continue|goose|openhands|openclaw|vibe|omp|droid|zcode in one command; undo with headroom unwrap <tool> . MCP server — headroom_compress , headroom_retrieve , headroom_stats for any MCP client. Cross-agent memory — one shared store across Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok, with automatic dedup. headroom learn — mines failed sessions and writes corrections to CLAUDE.local.md (default, gitignored), CLAUDE.md , AGENTS.md , GEMINI.md or GROK.md . Output token reduction — trims what the model writes back , not only what you send. See below . Reversible (CCR) — originals are cached locally and retrieved on demand. How it works Your agent / app
   (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, LangChain, Agno, Strands, your own code…)
        │   prompts · tool outputs · logs · RAG results · files
        ▼
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Headroom   (runs locally — your data stays here)  │
    │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
    │  CacheAligner  →  ContentRouter  →  CCR            │
    │                    ├─ SmartCrusher   (JSON)        │
    │                    ├─ CodeCompressor (AST)         │
    │                    └─ Kompress-v2-base (text, HF)  │
    │                                                    │
    │  Cross-agent memory  ·  headroom learn  ·  MCP     │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │   compressed prompt  +  retrieval tool
        ▼
 LLM provider  (Anthropic · OpenAI · Bedrock · …) ContentRouter detects the content type and selects a compressor for it. SmartCrusher / CodeCompressor / Kompress-v2-base handle JSON, source code and prose respectively. CacheAligner flags volatile content that would bust a provider KV-cache prefix. It never rewrites prompts. CCR stores originals locally so the model can call headroom_retrieve when it needs the full text. → Architecture · CCR · Kompress-v2-base model card Get started (60 seconds) # 1 — Install uv tool install --python 3.13 " headroom-ai[all] " # CLI in a self-contained env pip install " headroom-ai[all] " # Python — ships the `headroom` CLI npm install headroom-ai # TypeScript SDK only — no CLI # 2 — Pick a mode headroom deploy # turnkey local deployment + agent config headroom wrap claude # wrap a coding agent headroom proxy --port 8787 # drop-in proxy, zero code changes # or: from headroom import compress     # inline library # 3 — Check it and watch the savings headroom doctor # health check — confirms routing works headroom perf
headroom dashboard # live savings (proxy must be running) Reduce input tokens in your own app from headroom import compress from openai import OpenAI messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Analyze these results" }] result = compress ( messages , model = "gpt-4o" ) client = OpenAI () response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "gpt-4o" , messages = result . messages ) print ( f"Saved { result . tokens_saved } tokens ( { result . compression_ratio :.0% } )" ) Launch a wrapped agent session each time, so the setup runs. headroom wrap starts a local proxy and launches the agent configured to route through
Headroom. Add --code-memory serena to also install Serena for semantic code navigation (off
by default). For Claude Code, Serena is registered for the wrapped project only
(as a local -scope MCP server in ~/.claude.json ); use --code-memory-scope user to make it available in every project. headroom unwrap removes either registration. headroom wrap ... is session-scoped: its proxy exits with the wrapped agent.
For a proxy that survives reboots, use the turnkey headroom deploy command.
Use headroom install apply when you need to choose a specific persistent
service, scheduled task, Docker runtime, scope, or provider target; see the persistent installs guide . The headroom CLI ships only in the PyPI package. The npm headroom-ai package
is the TypeScript SDK — a library you import
( import { compress } from 'headroom-ai' ) — and provides no headroom command. Proof: measured token savings Four scenarios built from real MCP server output formats, measured with the
provider tokenizer and the shipped compress() at its default configuration.
Seeded and offline, so you get the same numbers we did: uv run python benchmarks/index_proof_table.py --seed 20260902 Scenario Before After Saved Code search (100 results) 17,199 13,597 21% SRE incident debugging 55,957 24,340 57% Codebase exploration 58,801 33,895 42% GitHub issue triage 46,067 32,429 30% Savings scale with how repetitive the payload is. Repeated JSON arrays and log
lines clear 90% in benchmarks/bench_latency.py ; prose and already-dense output
compress very little. Run headroom savings against your own traffic for the
number that applies to you. Compression costs well under a millisecond — 0.21 ms p50 on a 10K-token JSON
search result, 1.4 ms at 100K tokens — so it does not show up in agent latency. Accuracy. python -m headroom.evals suite --tier 1 : Benchmark Category N Baseline Headroom Delta GSM8K Math 100 0.870 0.870 ±0.000 TruthfulQA Factual 100 0.530 0.560 +0.030 SQuAD v2 QA 100 — 97% at 19% compression BFCL Tools 100 — 97% at 32% compression At N=100 a delta of ±0.03 falls inside the confidence interval, so TruthfulQA
shows no detectable difference rather than an improvement. Methodology → Output token reduction Everything above shrinks the prompt you send . You also pay for every token
the model writes back , and on Opus-class models output costs 5× input. Much
of that output is ceremony: "Great, let me…" preambles, code re-printed straight
back at you, and deep reasoning spent on routine steps like reading a file. github.title: a2ui-project/a2ui
github.abstract:
A2UI Build delightful, fast, reliable agentic experiences A2UI (Agent-to-User Interface) is an open-source generative UI framework,
complete with a protocol optimized for streaming dynamic user interfaces at
low latency, native renderers for web and mobile frameworks, and agent SDKs
in several popular languages. With A2UI, your agents can communicate with
your users using natively rendered widgets, in addition to text. Examples of UI compositions that A2UI can express. Quick links Main website . Try it in your browser using A2UI Composer . Supported renderers . Supported agents . Protocol specification . Introduction Large language models (LLMs) and decision models (e.g. Jev ) excel at creating text and code and at making
fast decisions on top of raw structured data (e.g. JSON). A2UI gives these
models a specialized vocabulary for expressing user interfaces. A2UI expresses UI using data , not code. A schema for the data exchanged
between the agent and the renderer enforces strict capability boundaries for
the agent, keeping agent-generated experiences safe and aligned with the
business requirements of your application. A core library , a native
framework adapter , and a catalog of components provide access to native
components and form the building blocks that the agent composes into a final
user experience, making the result expressive and high-performance. When to use A2UI Use A2UI when any of the following apply to your application: Parts of your application are agent- and/or server-driven. By design, A2UI
supports remote rendering. You want the UI to be composed dynamically, tailored to the user's immediate
need. Instead of making your users navigate through multiple screens to solve
their problems, have the agent build the right flow of UI that guides users
directly to solutions. You need the highest performance and visual fidelity. A2UI renders UI using
the framework of your choice, typically one that the host app itself is
written in. WebViews or HTML are not required. The same agent streams UI to multiple platforms or frameworks, such as
Flutter, React, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. A2UI helps keep the user
experience compatible and consistent across all screens. The agent is remote, third-party, or operates across a trust boundary. For
example, the agent must not be able to handle certain kinds of data (credit
card/account numbers, PII, financial data). A2UI helps enforce the trust
boundary and protect your app's critical functionality from hallucinations
using a strict schema, and by expressing UI using validated data rather than
executable code. A2UI core philosophy We develop A2UI under the guidance of the following core principles: Security first : The app developer controls what the agent can and cannot
do in the app. A2UI provides a framework for specifying and enforcing the
necessary guardrails, such as expressing UI as data, validating inputs and
outputs against a schema, and disallowing arbitrary executable code. Every
capability granted to the agent is either a safe standard capability built
into the framework, or a capability explicitly granted by the app developer. Model-friendly and server-driven : The A2UI protocol is designed to be
efficiently generated by language and decision models and transported over
the network, and to support progressive rendering (or "streaming") for a
responsive user experience. An agent can adapt the UI based on where the user
takes the conversation. A2UI supports swappable inference formats, so you can
tailor inference to specific models and use cases. Native rendering and portability : A2UI renders UI using the framework
native to your app, with renderers for many major UI frameworks. No need to
change frameworks unless required for other reasons. Architecture A2UI's architecture is made of multiple layers spanning the full stack that
connects the agent to the application: Inference : An agent (typically backed by a language or a decision model)
instructed by an A2UI skill (created using an A2UI Agent SDK) generates the
description of UI and data using an appropriate inference format (e.g. A2UI
Express, or a decision tree). Transport : An A2UI Agent SDK, embedded in a larger agent architecture,
parses and validates the model's output, expands macros, and converts the UI
to the wire-stable A2UI Transport protocol messages, which are sent to the
renderer. Rendering : A renderer is made of an A2UI Core library (e.g. the @a2ui/web_core npm package, or a2ui_core Dart package), a UI framework
adapter (e.g. @a2ui/react React adapter, or a2ui_flutter Flutter
adapter), and a widget catalog. The core library parses the incoming
messages and creates a framework-agnostic in-memory representation of the UI
and data. The framework adapter maps the in-memory representation to concrete
framework-specific UI widgets. The widget catalog provides access to the
widgets the agent is allowed to compose. Getting started Pick the path that matches where you want to start: Path What you get Time 🍜 Quickstart A full-stack A2UI app with a backend and frontend. Learn A2UI end-to-end and customize to your use case. ~5 min 🎨 A2UI Composer Generate A2UI JSON from a visual editor and paste it into any agent prompt — no install required. ~1 min 🎬 A2UI Theater Step through pre-built A2UI streaming scenarios across Lit, React, and Angular renderers — no install required. ~1 min Packages These packages are developed in this repository. Packages marked "Not published
yet" can be used from source. Python Package Description Version a2ui-core Protocol messages, data model, data binding, expression evaluation, and catalog validation. a2ui-agent-sdk Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. a2ui-a2a Connects the agent SDK to the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol . a2ui-adk Connects the agent SDK to the Agent Development Kit (ADK) . TypeScript Package Description Version @a2ui/web_core Protocol messages, state management, expressions, and basic catalog shared by renderers and @a2ui/agent . @a2ui/lit Lit (web components) renderer. @a2ui/angular Angular renderer. @a2ui/react React renderer. @a2ui/markdown-it Markdown rendering with markdown-it and DOMPurify, shared by the web renderers. @a2ui/agent Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. @a2ui/catalog-mcp MCP catalog: calls MCP tools and renders A2UI messages returned in tool results and UI resources. @a2ui/catalog-vegachart VegaChart catalog: renders Vega and Vega-Lite chart specifications on A2UI surfaces. Not published yet Dart and Flutter Package Description Version a2ui_core Protocol messages, data model, data binding, and expressions for renderers and agents. a2ui_agent Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. a2ui_flutter Flutter renderer. a2ui_cli Developer tool that generates typesafe component code from a catalog. GitHub Releases Swift The Swift libraries are distributed via Swift Package Manager from Package.swift at the root of this repository. Package Description A2UISwiftCore, BasicCatalog Message processor, data model, expression evaluation, and basic catalog definitions. A2UISwiftUI, BasicCatalogSwiftUI SwiftUI renderer and basic catalog views. Roadmap Protocol v1.1 : We are collecting requirements for the next iteration of
the A2UI protocol. Inference : Support for decision models (e.g. Jev). Templates : A cross-framework templating engine and a set of standard
primitives for rendering reusable rich UI widgets. Sandboxed logic : A way to securely attach logic to A2UI components. Agent SDK : Skill generation, better diagnostics, and integrations with
more agent frameworks. Evals : A set of tools for evaluating generated UI quality. MCP Apps : Embedding MCP Apps inside A2UI, and embedding A2UI experiences
into MCP Apps. CLI : Schema validation, codegen, local preview, and integration with
coding agents.

github.title: ModernRelay/omnigraph
github.abstract:
Object-storage native graph database with branching and typed ontology. Unified retrieval engine (vector/BM25/graph) · Git-style workflows · Open data format (Lance) Quickstart · Docs · Cookbooks · CLI · Studio · llms.txt Omnigraph is engineered for the new workload introduced by long-horizon agents: multiple agents sharing a typed world model to continuously retrieve and update context and coordinate work. Agents and UIs can become thin stateless consumers of durable state. Omnigraph Cloud is in private preview: join the waitlist . Join the Omnigraph Slack community to ask questions, share feedback, and follow development. Capabilities Capability What it gives you Typed ontology Agents share one enforceable model of the domain. .pg schemas declare node and edge types, keys and constraints, and the engine enforces them on every write. Multimodal retrieval Agents assemble high-precision & recall context in one query: graph traversal + vector ANN + full-text + Reciprocal Rank Fusion in one runtime, with filtering. Branching Agents propose reviewable changes instead of writing to main: a branch per agent or task, three-way merge, time travel across the whole graph. Declared as code A cluster.yaml declares graphs, schemas, stored queries, embedding providers and policies. cluster plan previews, cluster apply converges, Terraform-style. Security as code Cedar policy enforced server-side on every mutation , per graph or server-wide; bearer auth, server-resolved actors, audit tracking. Object-storage native, open format Decoupled storage and compute. Store graphs on local disk or S3-compatible storage: RustFS / MinIO, AWS S3 / R2, or Azure preview. Graph data uses open, versioned Lance , including Blob values. What you can build Use case What it's for Company brain Org knowledge unified into one graph every agent can query Agentic memory Durable, versioned memory: a branch per agent or per task, merged on review Context graph Decision traces and codified tribal knowledge for retrieval Dev graph Issues & dependency model that coding agents read and write R&D / ML data layer Experiments and trials written into branches, versioned for training & eval Install curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ModernRelay/omnigraph/main/scripts/install.sh | bash This installs omnigraph (CLI) and omnigraph-server into ~/.local/bin from
published release binaries. Or with Homebrew: brew tap ModernRelay/tap
brew install ModernRelay/tap/omnigraph Studio Omnigraph Studio is the desktop app for your graphs. Browse each type as
a table, follow relationships on a canvas, write queries with the compiler's
errors as you type, and review what a branch changes before you merge it. It is
a native Rust app on GPUI, the framework behind Zed, for macOS, Windows and Linux. Open a graph on one of your server targets in Studio: omnigraph studio --target < server > --graph < graph > Download Studio or read its source . Set it up with an AI agent Omnigraph is built to be run by coding agents. Two ways in: Teach your agent the playbook. The omnigraph binary carries the omnigraph agent skill written for it: the operational
playbook covering cluster mode, the two config surfaces, schema evolution, query
linting, data writes, branches, Cedar policy, and the common gotchas. Export it
where your agent loads skills, so the skill always matches the installed CLI: omnigraph skill export ~ /.claude/skills/omnigraph --force With an older CLI that has no skill command, or none installed, npx skills add ModernRelay/omnigraph@omnigraph installs the copy on the
default branch instead. Or have an agent set it up from scratch. Paste this into Claude Code,
Codex, or any agent that can read a URL and run a shell command: Read https://github.com/ModernRelay/omnigraph/blob/main/skills/omnigraph/references/onboarding.md and follow it to set up Omnigraph for me. The agent installs the CLI, asks what the graph is for, builds and queries a
small local graph, and then points to the cookbooks, a cluster or Omnigraph
Cloud. For ready-to-run graphs with real seed data (company brain, VC operating system,
pharma & industry intel), ModernRelay/omnigraph-cookbooks is the fastest way to see Omnigraph shaped to a real domain. Deploy A cluster declares graphs, schemas, stored queries, and policies in a
configuration bundle. cluster plan previews changes and cluster apply submits them to the selected destination. The cluster-only HTTP server exposes
graphs at /graphs/{id}/… and activates applied changes without a restart. Keep desired configuration separate from its destination: company-brain/
├── cluster.yaml
├── people.pg          # schema for the "knowledge" graph
├── queries/           # stored queries: the .gq files ARE the declaration
│   └── people.gq
├── cluster.policy.yaml # deployment permissions
└── graph.policy.yaml   # graph permissions # cluster.yaml version : 1 metadata : name : company-brain graphs : knowledge : schema : people.pg queries : queries/ # every `query <name>` in queries/*.gq registers policies : cluster-access : file : cluster.policy.yaml applies_to : [cluster] graph-access : file : graph.policy.yaml applies_to : [knowledge] For first boot, follow the cluster guide ,
including writer ownership transfer and authentication. The deployment guide covers containers and object stores;
Azure writers require its admission wrapper. The applied cluster policy must grant the authenticated operator config_manage .
Schema changes also require read and schema_apply on the affected graphs.
With those grants and a server target named production , deploy local edits: omnigraph cluster validate --config ./company-brain
omnigraph cluster plan --target production --config ./company-brain
omnigraph cluster apply --target production --config ./company-brain --config names the source bundle; --target names the destination. Omitting storage from the bundle uses the selected destination's root. If present, storage must match that root; it never selects or redirects the target.
Apply prints a deployment ID. If delivery is interrupted, inspect that ID
before submitting again; see deployment recovery . Query and mutate Define a server target with default_graph and set defaults.target once in ~/.omnigraph/config.yaml ( configuration ), and the
everyday commands stay short. Stored queries and mutations run by name : omnigraph query  search_docs --params ' {"q":"AI safety"} ' omnigraph mutate add_person  --params ' {"name":"Mina"} ' Branch, review and merge across the whole graph, so agents write in isolation: omnigraph branch create --from main agent/ingest-42
omnigraph branch merge  agent/ingest-42 --into main An alias is shorter still: bind a target, graph, and stored query to one
name, then omnigraph alias triage runs it. Data commands use --target NAME for a configured server or managed resource, plus --graph ID when needed.
Use --target ./graph.omni for a standalone local graph. Control-plane login
and organization operations use --profile ; see operator configuration . Security & governance Engine-wide enforcement: every write path goes through the same Cedar gate, so the HTTP server, the CLI, and the embedded SDK obey identical rules. Declared in the cluster: a policy bundle is bound to graphs (or the whole server) via policies: → applies_to . Scoped: rules apply per graph, per branch, or server-wide. Static server credentials: static bearer tokens are hashed at startup and compared in constant time. Forge-proof identity: the actor is resolved server-side from the token; clients can't set it. See the policy guide .

github.abstract:
The Context Database for AI Agents English / 中文 / 日本語 Website · Live Demo · GitHub · Issues · Docs · Blog Lark · WeChat · Discord · X What is OpenViking OpenViking is an open-source context database for AI agents — one filesystem for everything an agent knows: knowledge, memory, and skills. Most agent memory is a black box: text goes in, embeddings come out, and nobody can see what was actually stored. OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking:// instead. Agents navigate it like files — ls , tree , read , write , grep — and you can open any directory to inspect and edit what your agent knows. Every directory carries a generated summary, so agents can scan summaries first and decide what to read. Try OpenViking Studio in your browser, no installation required. Self-host Web Studio . Why OpenViking One filesystem for knowledge, memory, and skills. Resources hold documents and code; memories retain user preferences and experience; skills define how to perform tasks — not just extracted facts, but the full context, each with a viking:// URI for browsing and retrieval. → Viking URI · Context types Search a directory, not the whole index. Scope semantic search to a project or memory subtree instead of scanning a flat vector pool. find runs a query directly; search plans retrieval from session context. → Retrieval Read the summary before the source. Generated directory abstracts (L0) and overviews (L1) let agents judge relevance before opening full content (L2). → Context layers Sessions become files you can read. Committing a session archives the conversation and extracts memories as Markdown you can inspect, edit, and merge. With VikingBot enabled, ov compile organizes source material into a wiki, knowledge graph, or report. → Sessions · Context compilation Architecture · Design rationale viking://
├── resources/              # Resources: project docs, repos, web pages, etc.
│   └── my_project/
│       ├── docs/
│       │   ├── api/
│       │   └── tutorials/
│       └── src/
└── user/
    └── {user_id}/
        ├── memories/
        │   └── preferences/
        │       ├── writing_style
        │       └── coding_habits
        ├── resources/
        │   └── private_project/
        ├── skills/
        │   ├── search_code
        │   └── analyze_data
        └── peers/
            └── web-visitor-alice/ The three loading tiers: L0 (Abstract) : a one-sentence summary for quick relevance checks. L1 (Overview) : core information and usage scenarios for planning. L2 (Details) : the full original data, read only when needed. Semantically processed directories carry L0/L1 summaries, so agents can judge relevance before reading full files: viking://resources/my_project/
├── .abstract.md           # L0: quick relevance check
├── .overview.md           # L1: structure and key points
└── docs/
    ├── .abstract.md
    ├── .overview.md
    └── api/
        ├── auth.md         # L2: full content, loaded on demand
        └── endpoints.md Proof it works OpenViking 0.3.22 has been evaluated on long-conversation user memory (LoCoMo) and multi-turn agent tasks (tau2-bench). Full results and setup details, including knowledge-base QA, are in the benchmark report ; reproduction scripts live in ./benchmark . To run your own experiments, follow the RAG and Memory evaluation guide for routine VikingBot memory evaluation, published LoCoMo reproduction, separate mem0 prompt comparisons, and RAG evaluation. The memory evaluation used Doubao 2.0 Pro as the VLM and Doubao-embedding-vision-251215 as the embedding model. User memory (LoCoMo) : with OpenViking, all three agent integrations land at 80–83% accuracy — up from 24–57% on their native memory — while input tokens drop by 34.3–91.0% and query latency by 58.45–66.10%. Agent experience (tau2-bench) : experience memory lifts task success by +6.87pp (retail) and +11.87pp (airline) over the same LLM without memory. Quick start Set up an OpenViking server first; if you already have one, skip to Use it with your agent . Deploying your own needs uv, Python 3.10+ and a model provider with an embedding model and a VLM. Let your agent deploy it Follow this guide to install and start an OpenViking Server for me:

https://docs.openviking.ai/en/getting-started/04-setup-for-agent

Ask me for the model provider, the models, the workspace directory and whether
other machines need to reach the server; don't guess. When you ask for the model
API key, tell me how to hand it over if I'd rather not paste it into this chat,
and never repeat it back.

When it's running, tell me the server's address and whether auth is turned on. Your agent will first ask which model provider to use and for its API key. Deploy it yourself Install OpenViking and run the setup wizard, which configures the models: uv tool install openviking --upgrade && openviking-server init init writes ~/.openviking/ov.conf and supports Volcengine, OpenAI, Codex OAuth, Kimi, GLM and local Ollama; see the configuration guide . The server runs in the foreground, so keep this terminal open. Use OpenViking Service (hosted by Volcengine) The same OpenViking service, run for you by Volcengine. The first 50 files are free. Activate it on the Volcengine product page , then create an API key in the console under User Management → API Key. The server address is https://api.vikingdb.cn-beijing.volces.com/openviking ; you'll need it and the API key when you connect your agent. Explore with the CLI The openviking package includes the ov CLI. With the server running, import a repository and search it: ov status
ov add-resource https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking # Replace TASK_ID with the returned task_id; repeat until status is completed ov task status TASK_ID
ov ls viking://resources/
ov tree viking://resources/volcengine -L 2
ov find " what is openviking " ov grep " openviking " --uri viking://resources/volcengine/OpenViking/docs/en ov find returns matching context with URIs you can inspect. For client configuration ( ov config ), standalone CLI installs, and index maintenance, see CLI setup . Build your own integration with the Python , Go , or TypeScript SDK, or the HTTP API . Use it with your agent Connect your coding agent to OpenViking for cross-session memory. The memory plugin installer covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, TRAE, OpenCode and more, and detects which ones you have. Let your agent install it Install the OpenViking memory plugin and help me start using it. OpenViking is a context database for AI agents (https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking); the command and link below are from its official docs.

1. Run the official installer. It needs network access and writes to my home directory; if your sandbox blocks that, ask me for approval:
   curl -fsSL https://openviking.ai/install | bash -s -- --yes --lang en --url <SERVER_URL> --api-key <API_KEY>
2. Once it's installed, read the OpenViking onboarding guide and use it to walk me through setup. The guide has you ask me before choices like importing history or adding a working rule. docs.openviking.ai and docs.openviking.net are the same docs site; use whichever loads:
   https://docs.openviking.ai/agents/en/onboarding.md

The API key is a user key I created for myself on that server; the installer stores it in ~/.openviking/ovcli.conf on this machine. Use it in the command as it is; there's no need to show it in your replies, and don't write it into any other file or rule. Talk to me in English. Before you send it, replace <SERVER_URL> with your server's address and <API_KEY> with a user key; a root key can't read or write memories. If the server has auth turned off, use --api-key '' . Install it yourself Run the installer, then pick the tools and a server when asked: Self-hosted / local for a server on this machine, Volcengine OpenViking Cloud for OpenViking Service, or Custom URL for any other address. If auth is on, enter a user key, not the root key. curl -fsSL https://openviking.
